title: How Extreme Heat Harms the Body
hook: Your body cools itself by sweating — but in high heat and humidity, that system can be overwhelmed, and the result can be deadly. Knowing the signs is how you stay ahead of it.
key_points: The body sheds heat mainly by sweating; evaporation carries warmth away.
High humidity slows evaporation, so the cooling system stalls when you need it most.
When core temperature climbs unchecked, heatstroke — a medical emergency — can follow.
Hydrate, find shade or air conditioning, and avoid exertion during the hottest hours.
Check on older adults, young children, and anyone without cooling — they're most at risk.
content_html: A heat wave doesn't feel like an emergency the way a fire or a fall does — but excessive heat is one of the deadliest weather hazards, and it kills by quietly overwhelming the body's own cooling system. As NPR's Maria Godoy explains in an illustrated guide, understanding how that happens is the first step to staying safe.
extra_html:
The body sheds excess heat mainly by sweating: as sweat evaporates off the skin, it carries warmth away. That works well in dry air, but high humidity slows evaporation, so on hot, muggy days the cooling system stalls right when it's needed most. If core temperature keeps rising, the result can progress to heatstroke — a medical emergency that demands rapid cooling and a call for help.

The protective moves are straightforward: drink water before you feel thirsty, get into shade or air conditioning, and avoid hard exertion during the hottest part of the day. Just as important is looking out for the people most at risk — older adults, young children, and anyone without access to cooling — since they can overheat before they realize it.

related.title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarms
related.hook: Carbon monoxide is invisible and odorless. A working alarm is the only thing that will warn you before it's too late.

related.title: Preventing Falls at Home
related.hook: Falls are the leading cause of injury for older adults, but most are preventable with a few targeted fixes.

flashcards.prompt: Why does high humidity make extreme heat more dangerous?
flashcards.back_html: The body cools itself mainly by sweating — heat leaves as sweat evaporates. High humidity slows evaporation, so the body's cooling system can't keep up and core temperature can climb toward heatstroke.

flashcards.prompt: Which group is among the most vulnerable to extreme heat?

choices.text: Older adults and people without access to cooling
No one — bodies adjust automatically to any temperature

flashcards.explanation_html: The body's cooling has limits. Older adults, young children, and anyone without shade or air conditioning are at higher risk, which is why checking on them matters.
